The half-life rule: turning remaining life into a next inspection date

Short answer: Under API 510 (11th edition, 2022), remaining life = (actual thickness minus required thickness) divided by the corrosion rate, where t-required excludes corrosion allowance and mill tolerance. Unless an RBI assessment justifies otherwise, the interval to the next internal or on-stream inspection is the lesser of half the remaining life or 10 years. If remaining life is under four years, the interval may be the full remaining life, up to two years. The external visual interval is the lesser of five years or the internal interval.

The sections above explain how corrosion rate drives remaining life. This section takes the last step that auditors and inspectors check first: turning a remaining-life number into a dated next inspection, using the rules as API 510 states them. The equipment-specific rules for piping and tanks are covered after the vessel rules. API codes are copyrighted, so everything here is paraphrased. Clause references are to the API 510 11th edition (October 2022, with errata in 2023 and 2025). Confirm against the edition your programme adopts. The interval is set by the inspector or engineer under the owner-operator's quality assurance system. NDE data feeds that decision but does not make it.

What API 510 actually says about remaining life

API 510 calculates remaining life in years as actual thickness minus required thickness, divided by the corrosion rate. Each term has a precise meaning in the code, and most errors come from using a near-miss definition:

  • Actual thickness is the thickness measured at a corrosion monitoring location (CML) during the most recent inspection.
  • Required thickness is the minimum thickness for the same CML or component, from the design formulas for pressure and structural loads, without corrosion allowance or manufacturer's tolerances. API 510 also lets it be reassessed through a fitness-for-service analysis under API 579-1/ASME FFS-1. That is an engineering assessment the owner commissions, not a default.
  • Corrosion rate is the rate the inspector selects, in consultation with a corrosion specialist, as best reflecting current conditions.

API 510 defines two rate calculations. The long-term rate uses the initial thickness at the CML and the current reading. The initial thickness is either the first measurement at that CML or the thickness at the start of a new corrosion environment. The short-term rate uses the previous and current readings. The code does not simply say "always use the higher." It lists factors to weigh when choosing:

  • whether damage is general or localized
  • impingement or erosion-corrosion
  • when the corrosion started
  • process changes such as water wetting, chlorides or lower pH
  • whether protective scale has formed or been stripped away
  • stagnant areas where deposits such as iron sulfide collect
  • whether the unit keeps operating within its integrity operating windows
  • whether a short-term spike came from a one-off event that has since been corrected

Choosing the higher rate, as described earlier on this page, is the conservative default many programmes adopt. The code's own test is which rate best reflects current conditions, and the choice must be documented.

API 510 also stresses data quality. Thickness and corrosion-rate data used for remaining life should be validated before they set next inspection dates. Bad data raises the risk of unexpected failure or of retiring a vessel too early. A statistical treatment of thickness data is allowed but must be documented. It may not suit vessels with random but significant localized corrosion.

The interval rules, in plain language

Inspection type (API 510)Default maximum interval, unless RBI justifies otherwiseNotes
Internal or on-stream inspectionThe lesser of half the remaining life or 10 yearsAn internal is not required at half the remaining life where thinning can be detected or monitored effectively from outside.
Thickness measurement inspectionThe lesser of half the remaining life or 10 yearsThe same short-remaining-life provision applies.
Remaining life under four yearsMay be the full remaining life, up to a maximum of two yearsApplies to both internal/on-stream and thickness intervals.
External visual inspection (aboveground vessels)The lesser of five years or the required internal/on-stream intervalPreferably done with the vessel in operation.
Projected-MAWP method (alternative)The interval works if the projected MAWP of the limiting component stays at or above the nameplate or rerated MAWP plus static head. Still capped at 10 years without RBI.Iterative: choose an interval, project the metal loss, then check MAWP.
RBI-based intervalsMay exceed the 10-year and half-life limits for internal and on-stream inspections and the 5-year external limitRBI-based external intervals must not exceed 10 years. An RBI interval beyond 10 years needs engineer and inspector review at least every 10 years.

Two points are easy to miss. First, the half-life rule is a ceiling, not a target. API 510 separately warns that when corrosion rates speed up or become unstable, the cause should be investigated using API RP 585. It also warns that relying on ever-shorter inspection intervals can be a riskier strategy than replacement, redesign or a material upgrade. Second, vessels in non-continuous service can count years of actual operation rather than calendar years. This applies only if, while idle, the vessel is isolated from process fluids and protected from corrosive internal environments.

Worked example 1: a vessel shell with a long remaining life

These figures are illustrative. Real values come from your design calculations and CML history.

  • CML on the lower shell course of a carbon steel drum. t-required for that course, from the construction-code formula without corrosion allowance: 0.420 in.
  • First reading at this CML (2006): 0.625 in. Previous reading (2020): 0.560 in. Current reading (2026): 0.540 in.
  • Long-term rate: (0.625 - 0.540) / 20 years = 0.00425 in./yr (4.25 mpy).
  • Short-term rate: (0.560 - 0.540) / 6 years = 0.0033 in./yr (3.3 mpy).
  • The inspector, with the corrosion specialist, finds no process change and uniform thinning. To stay conservative they select the long-term rate, 4.25 mpy, and record why.
  • Remaining life: (0.540 - 0.420) / 0.00425 = 28.2 years.
  • Half the remaining life is 14.1 years, which exceeds 10 years. The next internal or on-stream inspection is therefore due within 10 years, by 2036.
  • External visual: the lesser of five years or the internal interval, so due by 2031.
  • MAWP check for continued service: API 510 calculates MAWP using measured thickness minus twice the expected corrosion loss before the next inspection. That gives 0.540 - 2 x (0.00425 x 10) = 0.455 in., still above 0.420 in. The current MAWP is supported through 2036.

The governing date for the vessel is the shortest result across all its CMLs and components, not the shell alone. As noted earlier on this page, that is often a nozzle.

Worked example 2: a nozzle with less than four years left

  • Inlet nozzle CML with erosion-corrosion. t-required 0.270 in. Current reading 0.300 in. Selected rate 9 mpy (0.009 in./yr), from the short-term rate because the attack is localized and recent.
  • Remaining life: (0.300 - 0.270) / 0.009 = 3.3 years.
  • Remaining life is under four years, so API 510 allows the interval to be the full remaining life up to a maximum of two years. Half-life would give 1.67 years.
  • Now apply the MAWP projection. At a two-year interval, projected thickness = 0.300 - 2 x (0.009 x 2) = 0.264 in. That is below the 0.270 in. required. A two-year interval would not support the current MAWP. To keep projected thickness at or above 0.270 in., the interval must be no more than (0.300 - 0.270) / (2 x 0.009) = 1.67 years.
  • The decision belongs to the inspector and engineer. Options include a shorter interval, on-stream monitoring of the nozzle, a repair or replacement plan, or an owner-commissioned engineering assessment. The record must show which option was chosen and why.

This example shows why a remaining-life spreadsheet with only one formula is not enough. The two-year short-life allowance, the half-life ceiling and the MAWP projection can each give a different answer. The programme has to show which one governs.

Same logic in API 570 and API 653, different caps

API 570 (piping). The current edition (5th, February 2024) calculates remaining life in its section on remaining life. Interval setting is in its inspection-interval section, with a table of maximum intervals by piping class. API's own Body of Knowledge for the API 570 exam cites remaining life at 7.2 and intervals at 6.3.3 and Table 1. Thickness-measurement intervals follow the same principle: the lesser of half the remaining life or the class maximum in that table, plus separate rules for injection points and soil-to-air interfaces. Take the class-maximum figures from your licensed copy of the current edition. For class-specific detail see API 570 Class 1 inspection intervals and piping circuit CML inspection.

API 653 (tanks). Tank intervals use component-specific logic. Shell and bottom are treated differently, with bottom remaining life based on minimum remaining thickness after projected product-side and soil-side corrosion. External inspection intervals are tied to the shell corrosion rate, and internal intervals to projected bottom thickness, each with code maximums. API 653 Addendum 4 (July 2025) revised the text on tank-bottom thickness measurement, so check the current edition and addendum before quoting numbers. See API 653 tank inspection intervals explained.

Across all three codes, an RBI assessment under API RP 580 or 581 can justify different intervals. That is an owner-commissioned engineering assessment with its own documentation and review requirements, not a shortcut. For the trade-offs see time-based vs risk-based intervals.

New vessels, service changes and "no corrosion rate yet"

Remaining life needs a corrosion rate. New vessels, and vessels moved to a new service, do not have one yet. API 510 gives four ways to estimate a probable rate:

  1. Data from the owner's own vessels in the same or similar service.
  2. Readings from appropriately placed ultrasonic sensors.
  3. An estimate from a corrosion specialist.
  4. Published data for similar service.

Where none of these can be applied with confidence, the inspection plan must include on-stream direct measurement of wall loss after six months of service. Measurements continue at suitable intervals until a credible rate is established. API 510 notes that thickness readings taken over short intervals carry statistical scatter, so an early "rate" may not reflect the environment. If the assumed rate later proves wrong, the actual rate must replace it in the remaining-life calculation. That changes the next inspection date as well.

For large vessels with zones that corrode at clearly different rates, API 510 allows each zone to be treated on its own, with its own interval. It also lets a qualified corrosion specialist document that a vessel has no credible internal degradation mechanism. That vessel may then be exempt from internal inspection and corrosion monitoring. External inspection is still required.

Deferring a due date without breaking the rules

A calculated date is binding. The API 510 11th edition says a vessel may not be operated past its due date without a valid deferral. Deferrals must be documented and are meant to be the exception. A simplified deferral may be approved by the owner-operator only if all of the following are true:

  • The due date has not been deferred before.
  • The new date adds no more than 10 percent of the interval or six months, whichever is less.
  • A review of operating conditions and history supports it.
  • The owner's inspector and operations management consent.
  • The records are updated before the original due date passes.

Anything longer needs a documented risk assessment, or an update to an existing RBI assessment, under a formal deferral procedure. Calculated remaining life is one of the inputs that procedure considers.

The record an inspector or auditor expects

For each component or CML group, a defensible next-inspection-date record shows:

  • the t-required calculation and its code basis, without corrosion allowance
  • the thickness history at consistent CMLs, with method and instrument details
  • the long-term and short-term rates, the rate selected and the reasoning
  • the remaining life
  • which interval rule governs: half-life, 10-year cap, short-life allowance, MAWP projection or RBI
  • the resulting internal, thickness and external due dates
  • the name of the inspector or engineer who set them under the owner's QA system

At PSM-covered US facilities, 29 CFR 1910.119(j) also requires each inspection and test to be documented with the date, the person who did it, the equipment identifier, a description and the results. In Alberta, ABSA's AB-506 sets provincial interval and documentation requirements that apply alongside API 510. For PSM support see OSHA PSM mechanical integrity NDT.

Common half-life mistakes

  • Calculating to nominal minus corrosion allowance. Remaining life should be calculated to the required thickness, not to nominal thickness less the corrosion allowance. Mixing the two can either inflate or deflate remaining life.
  • Using remaining life itself as the interval. The interval is half the remaining life, capped. The full-remaining-life allowance applies only below four years and only up to two years.
  • Applying the 10-year cap to external inspection. The external cap is five years, or the internal interval if shorter, unless RBI justifies otherwise.
  • Ignoring the MAWP projection. As worked example 2 shows, it can govern for short-life components.
  • Letting dates slip because the rate "looks wrong". Investigate the data, but keep the date unless a documented deferral is in place.
  • Resetting the long-term rate after a repair without documenting a new corrosion environment. API 510 allows a new initial thickness only at the start of a new corrosion environment.

Half-life rule FAQs

What is remaining life in pressure vessel inspection?

It is the years left before a component reaches its required thickness at the selected corrosion rate. It equals actual minus required thickness, divided by the corrosion rate.

What is the half remaining life inspection interval?

API 510 caps the interval between internal or on-stream inspections at the lesser of half the remaining life or 10 years, unless RBI justifies otherwise.

What if remaining life is less than four years?

The interval may be the full remaining life, up to a maximum of two years. Check the MAWP projection too, because it can be tighter.

Does t-required include corrosion allowance?

No. API 510 defines required thickness without corrosion allowance or manufacturer's tolerances.

Which corrosion rate should I use, long-term or short-term?

The one that best reflects current conditions, chosen by the inspector with a corrosion specialist and documented. Many programmes default to the higher of the two.

How is the API 570 next inspection date calculated?

The same way in principle: the lesser of half the remaining life or the class maximum in API 570's interval table. Use the current 5th edition figures.

Can an RBI assessment replace the half-life rule?

Yes. API 510 allows RBI under API RP 580 to set intervals beyond the half-life and 10-year limits, with required periodic review. It is an engineering assessment the owner commissions.
